sections.html:
Hancock County sits on the Ohio River on Kentucky's northwest side, inside the Owensboro metro area. Hawesville is the seat and Lewisport is the largest town. The 2020 count was 9,095 residents and the July 2025 estimate is 9,050, with 3,968 housing units. Owners hold 77.2 percent of households, the typical owned home is valued at $141,200, and typical rent is $740. Only 15 building permits were counted for 2025, so a Hancock County seller is usually offering a resale house in a small market where new construction rarely sets the price.

With a typical home near $141,200, a few years of missed tax bills plus penalties can take a visible bite out of a sale price, which is why it pays to settle the account before listing.

Three offices share the Hancock County Administration Building at 225 Main Cross Street in Hawesville, and each has a separate job.

  • Sheriff, first floor: takes payment. Phone 270-927-6247, mail to P.O. Box 427. Posted hours are 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays.
  • PVA: values property and has no say over rates or payments. It reads the market each January 1 and aims for what a willing buyer would pay. Phone 270-927-6846, mail to P.O. Box 523.
  • County Clerk, second floor: keeps land records and processes delinquent real estate taxes. Phone 270-927-6117, mail to P.O. Box 146.

The state Department of Revenue supervises the PVA and runs yearly studies in every county to check that assessments meet constitutional standards.

Bills reach the sheriff by mid September. Until then the PVA mails the current-year bill to whatever in-care-of address appears in the deed. KRS 134.015 sets the discount and face-value windows.

Payment windows for a Hancock County bill
Payment windowWhat you owe
On or before November 1Face amount less a 2 percent discount
Rest of the yearFace amount
January5 percent penalty added
After January 3110 percent penalty plus a 10 percent sheriff fee, described by the state as 21 percent combined

When the state delays mailing, an alternative schedule gives 30 days per stage. The bill in your hand carries the dates that apply. Whoever owned the house on January 1 is the taxpayer of record for that year, so a closing in October or November is the moment to ask the sheriff for the exact discount cutoff.

Rental property owners, farmers and home-based businesses with activity in Hancock County pay an occupational tax on net profits. The rate on business profits has been 1.60 percent since January 1, 2020, and an annual business license costs $10.

Employees working inside the county pay 1.60 percent of gross wages, withheld by the employer. Two exceptions apply: a company employing more than 100 people in manufacturing in the county does not owe the net profits fee, and neither does a business that pays the county a franchise tax.

A landlord selling a Hancock County rental should expect a net profits return for the year of the sale. The Occupational Tax Office, on the third floor, answers at 270-927-8788.

Meet the PVA first. Call 270-927-6846 to book a conference in the spring inspection window, which no appeal can skip. If the talk ends without a deal, you have one workday after the window closes to file with the clerk upstairs, along with the value you claim.

A three-person local appeals board hears the case about five weeks later and expects evidence from you. The Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals hears anything further. Ask the PVA which sales it relied on, then bring your own comparable sales.

Owners aged 65 and up, and owners classified as totally disabled, can ask the PVA to lower the taxable value of their own residence. KRS 132.810 allows one exemption per household unit and treats a manufactured house as a unit. After a sale, the old owner reports the transfer and the new owner applies separately. Ask the PVA for the dollar figure in force.

sections.h2: Timing a sale around the tax year
sections.html:
The bill covers a full calendar year and is owed by whoever held the house on January 1, so the seller normally carries it even after a fall closing. Many contracts split it at the table. Ask your closing agent how yours does.

If you list in spring, check where the bill stands before April 15, because after that date the clerk holds it and charges add up. If you list in summer, certificate sales begin in July, so settle any open balance first. A seller with several unpaid years and a house that needs work may find that a cash buyer buying as is can close fast enough to pay everything off from the proceeds, without repairs or lender delays.

A short checklist keeps surprises away from the table.

  • Confirm the deed carries a mailing address for the new owner's tax bill, which KRS 382.135 requires.
  • Ask the sheriff whether a current-year bill is open and who will pay it, since the bill covers a full calendar year.
  • Search the parcel through the clerk's website, which links a delinquent tax tool (DTax) and eCCLIX, a viewer for filed land records that helps when a house came through an estate.
  • Pull permits for any addition. Planning and Zoning is at 200 Court Square, P.O. Box 692, open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 8 a.m. to noon at 270-927-8169.

The Hancock County Urban Planning Commission holds evening meetings every other month, starting the first Monday of February.

sections.h2: What happens to an unpaid bill?
sections.html:
A bill still open when April 15 ends leaves the sheriff and lands with the clerk as a certificate of delinquency. The clerk's DTax tool shows what the county believes is owed on a parcel, and the clerk sets the true figure at payment or sale. Interest, a clerk commission and later an attorney commission pile on, and a buyer of the certificate adds more. A seller who plans to list in summer should pay or collect a written payoff before certificate sales begin in July.

Back taxes do not block a sale. The settlement agent pays the payoff from the proceeds, the same way it works with a cash buyer who purchases as is. Ask the clerk for the payoff in writing, dated close to the closing day, because interest keeps accruing.

faqs.q: Do rental owners in Hancock County pay occupational tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Rental property owners pay on net profits at 1.60 percent, plus a $10 annual business license. The Occupational Tax Office at 270-927-8788 takes the forms.

faqs.q: When does the Hancock County Urban Planning Commission meet?
faqs.a: Every other month, starting with the first Monday of February. Meetings begin at 7 p.m. on the third floor of the Administration Building, 225 Main Cross Street.

faqs.q: How can I view recorded deeds for a Hancock County house?
faqs.a: Through eCCLIX on the County Clerk's website, which lets you view or print filed documents. Questions go to 270-927-6117.

faqs.q: I bought a Hancock County home and never got a tax bill. Who do I call?
faqs.a: The sheriff at 270-927-6247 can provide a copy. The PVA mails the bill to the address in the deed until preparation begins in mid September, which is why that address matters.

faqs.q: Is the PVA or the sheriff the office that takes the payment?
faqs.a: The sheriff. The PVA's role ends at valuation, and payments go to the Hancock County Sheriff's Office on the first floor.
